title: How a restaurant group should write an about page
metaTitle: How a restaurant group writes an about page
excerpt: Name who cooks and who runs the room, and why a guest tonight should care. Keep the origin story only when it changes the decision to open the menu or book.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, a small still life that suggests makers without telling you who is cooking tonight.
caption: Bottles on a table, and no one standing behind them yet. The about page still needs a name. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on a restaurant group's about page?
faqs.answer: The people a guest might meet or rely on: the chef for that room, the person who runs the floor, and the kind of night the group actually serves. A short note on how the rooms relate is enough. A skyline and a founding year do not tell anyone where to eat.

faqs.question: Should we tell the origin story?
faqs.answer: Tell it only when a detail changes the booking. A chef who still writes the dinner menu, or a room that stayed small on purpose, can matter. The year two friends signed a lease usually does not. If the story does not help someone choose a table, save it for a talk.

faqs.question: How do we write about several restaurants?
faqs.answer: Give each room a few lines and a person, then one sentence on what the group shares. Do not dissolve the rooms into a single myth. A guest books a door, not a holding company. Link each room to its menu and its table.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A restaurant group about page is proof that specific people stand behind dinner. Name who cooks and who runs the room, and why a guest deciding where to go tonight should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes their decision to see the menu or book a table.

The homepage already showed a room and a dish. This page shows custody. Who is on the pass. Who will notice the table. A lease story and a city photograph do not answer that.

## Names before the myth

Open on a person a guest might rely on. The chef of the room you are featuring, or the operator who is actually in the building. "Mina runs the kitchen at Holt Street and writes the dinner menu" is an about page working. "We are passionate about gathering" is a poster.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) puts weight on who created the work, and on whether a visitor can see the expertise. A restaurant is not an essay, but the test holds. If the only name on the site is the group, a careful guest has to guess who is cooking. Some will not guess. They will book the place that names a person.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for a descriptive, concise title and a clear heading. "About" is a habit. "Who cooks, and who is in the room" is a summary. Use the plainer heading if you will stand behind it. Keep the browser title specific so it is not a second homepage.

Do not open on bottles, a skyline, or a handshake you rented. Those frames have no shift and no pass. If you need a picture first, use the kitchen or the floor during service, with names in text beside it. The reader is choosing dinner, not admiring glass.

## Who does the work

List people in the order a guest feels them. The room they might book. The person responsible for the food there. The person responsible for the floor. If one human wears two of those, say so. Small groups lose trust when the website implies a crowd of executive chefs and the room has one.

For each person, three lines:

- Name and role.
- Which restaurant they are in tonight, or which ones they move between.
- What they actually decide: the menu, the wine, the bookings, the room.

Skip hobbies unless they change dinner. A chef who dry-ages in house has a fact. A chef who loves surfing does not, on this page. Be a full person in the room. The page is a decision tool.

Keep the list current. A chef who left six months ago is a trust break the moment a regular notices. Names should be editable text, not a poster from the rebrand. Portraits can be plain. A true photograph in the kitchen beats a campaign still that hides the stove.

Group shots can sit beside the list. They cannot replace names. A reader cannot learn who writes the menu by squinting at a lineup. Put the name in type.

## Why a guest tonight should care

Taste and hunger got them here. The about page connects these people to this night. That means the kind of cooking, the size of the room, and whether the person named is actually present. "We care about produce" is available to every group. "The chef who plates the leek is the one who wrote the menu this morning" is a reason.

Write two or three sentences only your group could sign. The room that stayed at thirty seats. The decision to run two kitchens instead of one brand stretched thin. The neighborhood you cook for, in the sense of who walks in. If a sentence still works with a competitor's name pasted in, cut it.

Point at the food and the room. "This is the Holt Street menu Mina wrote" with a link is stronger than a paragraph of adjectives. The about page can be short because the restaurants themselves are the proof. Its job is to attach names.

Say the limit. If you do not take walk-ins, or you do not do cakes, or one room is a wine bar and not a dinner destination, say it in human form. The right guest relaxes. The wrong guest books somewhere else before the disappointment. Both are good.

A guest deciding tonight may only need the name and the link to book. Do not trap them in the myth on the way to the button. Put Menu and Book where a thumb can reach them. The about page that hides the table has forgotten its reader.

## When the origin earns a paragraph

Most origin stories do not change a booking. Two friends, a stubborn landlord, a city that was different then. None of that tells a guest whether they can get a table at eight.

Keep a detail when it predicts the night. You opened as a day cafe and the room still stops dinner at ten, on purpose. The chef came from a bakery and the bread is still made downstairs. The group refused a fourth site so the named chefs stay in the buildings. The story is allowed because it is evidence, not because it is charming.

Put that detail after the names. Readers who want the myth can have it. Readers who want to know if the chef is in the building should not have to survive 2009 first. A page that begins with the lease and mentions dinner in paragraph six has the order backwards.

If the interesting history is the room itself, show the room and link to it. Let service carry the past. You do not need to novelize the fit-out.

Read the story to someone choosing dinner and ask what they would do differently. If the answer is nothing, the story is for you. Keep it for the staff meal. Take it off the page that should open a menu.

## Several rooms, one group

Say what is shared in one sentence. A family of kitchens. A single bakery that feeds three rooms. A booking desk. Then stop merging them. Each restaurant needs its own lines, its own person, and its own link to menu and table.

A guest who liked one room may be curious about the others. Give them the difference, not a slogan that flattens it. "Quieter, shorter menu, no cocktails" is a useful difference. "The same soul" is not. Soul can be true and still unusable at 6:40 p.m.

Do not rank the rooms on the about page. Ranking creates a flagship and two afterthoughts, and the afterthoughts still need to fill seats. Describe them. Let the guest rank.

Press and awards can follow, attached to the room that earned them. A logo wall at the top is the myth in another costume. The guest still needs a name and a door.

## A page the floor can keep true

Chefs move. Hours change. The page has to be editable without a photoshoot. Name, role, restaurant, paragraph, portrait. A custom layout is welcome. A flattened campaign image is how the page starts lying.

Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for the standard of a public page that stays specific: a real subject, a real constraint, words beside the picture. A restaurant about page is that standard applied to people. Hanabi designs and builds sites where those words stay editable after launch. The studio will not invent a founding quote for you.

Keep the voice identical to the menu and the captions. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. If the menu says "grilled leek" and the about page says "a dialogue with fire," you have two restaurants. Pick the one the guest will eat.

Check the page on a phone. The first screen should show a person and a room, plus a way to the menu or a table. An about page that only works as a desktop essay has forgotten the guest in the group chat.

Ask a friend who has eaten with you once to read only this page and say which room they would book, and who they think is cooking. If they recite the lease and miss the chef, the myth is still in the way. Move the names up. If they cannot find the menu, the page is a dead end and the button is too shy. Fix those two things before you commission another portrait. The guest tonight needs a person and a door. The portrait can improve later. A correct name in ordinary light is already enough to trust.

## The night those people can point to

Names without a room slide back into claim. Once a reader knows who is cooking, they will want one night told properly: the constraint, the decision, and the room with one dish. That is a proof page, not another paragraph of biography.

Read [proof pages for a restaurant group](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-restaurant-group) next. The about page attaches a person to the door. The proof page shows the judgment behind a specific service, so a similar guest can decide to book. Keep the names you just wrote nearby when you draft that proof. A dish without a person, and a person without a dish, are both unfinished.
